memory_leads.lead: Social welfare at sea is an availability-and-access system, not merely a benefit category. Family contact, private communication, peer/community support, shore access and trusted help channels can remain unavailable in practice even when a nominal service or policy exists.

Onboard communications have several separate states: technical link availability, crew access, usable bandwidth/latency, affordability or allowance, device/time access and privacy. A vessel can be technically connected while individual seafarers still have weak practical contact with home.

Family contact is part of tour sustainability. Long separation, time-zone mismatch, family emergencies and uncertain relief dates can create background cognitive load; communication can reduce isolation but cannot substitute for predictable rotation or physical presence.

Social isolation can exist inside a fully crewed vessel. Watch schedules, department boundaries, language groups, rank hierarchy and individual cabin patterns can reduce shared time, so co-location is not equivalent to social support.

Peer support and informal buddy networks are a resilience layer distinct from formal medical or HR channels. Early signs of distress, conflict or overload may first be noticed by shipmates, but usefulness depends on trust, time, confidentiality and willingness to intervene.

Multinational and multilingual crews can gain diversity and broad experience while also facing belonging and communication friction. Shared working language does not guarantee social inclusion; off-watch language, food, humor, hierarchy and cultural assumptions can shape cohesion.

Shore leave and shore access are recovery opportunities rather than a binary legal entitlement in this Memory model. Port-stay length, workload, transport, terminal location, security, documentation and local access constraints can make nominal opportunity unusable; exact rights and restrictions require Evidence.

Port-side welfare support forms a shore interface that may include transport, communication access, practical assistance, counseling/chaplaincy-type support and emergency help. Its structural role is to bridge a transient crew to local services; named organizations and capabilities require Evidence.

Harassment, bullying, discrimination and interpersonal intimidation are welfare and operational risks because they can degrade concentration, team communication and willingness to report errors or hazards. The structural category should be preserved without inferring any specific legal finding or incident.

Reporting interpersonal problems is shaped by power asymmetry. Rank, appraisal, contract renewal, crewing-agency relationships and fear of retaliation can affect whether a concern is raised, to whom, and when; a formal complaint route does not prove psychological safety.

Privacy is a welfare resource. Private calls/messages, confidential support or complaint channels and physical conversational privacy can be limited by shared spaces, monitored systems or close-knit crews, changing whether support is actually usable.

Shared meals, recreation, exercise, celebrations and routine communal activities can build cohesion and provide non-work identity. Their value depends on actual participation and schedule compatibility rather than the mere presence of facilities.

Connectivity has a two-sided operational effect. Better contact can support family ties and welfare, while constant messaging, bad news from home or off-watch screen use can also intrude on rest or attention; replay should preserve the communication state without assuming a uniformly positive or negative effect.

P033 employment/welfare and retention are refined because the experienced employment package includes social connection, predictable access to home and trusted support, not only wages, rotation and formal benefits.

P036 health-readiness is refined by separating clinical/medical support from non-clinical social support. Isolation, family stress or interpersonal conflict may affect readiness and help-seeking without constituting a diagnosis.

P032 safety culture is refined because willingness to challenge, report or ask for help depends partly on interpersonal trust and retaliation risk; formal reporting procedures alone do not establish a speak-up environment.

P037 common/recreation spaces are refined because physical availability is only one layer; schedule overlap, social inclusion, privacy and voluntary participation determine whether those spaces actually produce recovery or cohesion.
The atlas already identifies labor/crewing and private/regional histories as under-recalled; P038 supplies social-welfare operating states rather than repeating the broad negative-space statement.

Generic Memory-not-Evidence, known-time and uncertainty semantics are already Baseline rules; P038 applies them to welfare access, interpersonal conditions and reporting states that are particularly vulnerable to hindsight and unverifiable anecdote.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Specific services, prices, allowances and technical capabilities vary by vessel/company/time and require dated Evidence.
Blind memory supports shore-access constraints structurally but not legal rights, port/jurisdiction rules or exact historical implementation.
Individual allegations, findings and remedies require claim-scoped Evidence and must not be inferred from structural Memory.
Named-provider/program capability and current availability are directory-like and time-sensitive and require source-first research.

stop_reason: The non-physical welfare chain is populated from practical connectivity/family contact through isolation, peer/community support, shore access, privacy and interpersonal mistreatment/reporting dynamics. Further recall becomes service-, cost-, policy-, right-, case-, provider-, program- or jurisdiction-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no connectivity service level, shore-leave entitlement, harassment/bullying finding, mental-health diagnosis, welfare-provider capability, complaint outcome or current crew social condition is verified.
